solutions.latex:
$$\frac{dy}{dx}=4x^3+6x^2$$

Let $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ 4x^3+6x^2&=0\\2x^2(2x+3)&=0\\ \therefore\ x&=0,-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$

$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=12x^2+12x$$

When $x=0$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0\Longrightarrow$ inconclusive; use table

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-1&0&1\\\hline f'(x)&2&0&10\\ &\nearrow&\rightarrow&\nearrow\end{array}$$

$\therefore(0,1)$ is a horizontal point of inflexion.

When $x=-\dfrac{3}{2}$, $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=9>0\Longrightarrow\left(-\dfrac{3}{2},-\dfrac{11}{16}\right)$ is a minimum turning point.

Let $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=0$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ 12x^2+12x&=0\\12x(x+1)&=0\\ \therefore\ x&=0,-1\end{aligned}$$

Already established there is a point of inflection at $x=0$.

Check whether there is a point of inflection at $x=-1$:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&-2&-1&-0.5\\\hline f''(x)&24&0&-3\\ &+&&-\end{array}$$

$\therefore(-1,0)$ is a point of inflection.

\exfigure{1313_q21_s1}

From the graph, global maximum $=4$.

solutions.latex:
$$I=\frac{k^2y^2}{(y^2+a^2)^3}$$

$$\begin{aligned}\frac{dI}{dy}&=\frac{(y^2+a^2)^3\cdot2k^2y-k^2y^2\cdot3(y^2+a^2)^2\cdot2y}{(y^2+a^2)^6}\\&=\frac{2k^2y(y^2+a^2)^3-6k^2y^3(y^2+a^2)^2}{(y^2+a^2)^6}\\&=\frac{2k^2y(y^2+a^2)^2\left[(y^2+a^2)-3y^2\right]}{(y^2+a^2)^6}\\&=\frac{2k^2y(a^2-2y^2)}{(y^2+a^2)^4}\end{aligned}$$

Let $\dfrac{dI}{dy}=0$

$$\begin{aligned}\therefore\ 2k^2y(a^2-2y^2)&=0\\ \therefore\ y&=0,\pm\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\\ \therefore\ y&=0,\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\text{ (as }y\ge0)\end{aligned}$$

But $y=0$ provides no illumination to the circumference.

$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}y&\frac{a}{2}&\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}&a\\\hline\frac{dI}{dy}&\frac{2k^2\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)\left(\frac{a^2}{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{a^2}{4}+a^2\right)^4}&0&\frac{2k^2a(-a^2)}{(a^2+a^2)^4}\\ &\nearrow&\rightarrow&\searrow\end{array}$$

$\therefore\ y=\dfrac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ provides the maximum illumination to the circumference.
solutions.marks_breakdown: 1: finding $\frac{dI}{dx}$, or equivalent merit; 1: obtaining $y=0,\pm\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$; 1: proving that $y=\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}$ provides the maximum illumination to the circumference
